title: T1568.003 — Dynamic Resolution - DNS Calculation
subtitle: Watch a full DNS Calculation round trip: the implant asks one harmless-looking DNS question, the attacker’s name server answers with a crafted IP address, the implant computes...

nodes.label: Sensitive data
nodes.tip: Sensitive data - What is at risk

steps.title: The implant needs orders
steps.caption: Malware on the victim laptop wakes up. Its main command-and-control address is blocked by the company’s egress firewall, so it falls back to a hardcoded attacker domain, update-svc.c2tld[.]com . Nothing has crossed the network yet
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: The DNS question leaves the host
steps.caption: The implant asks the company resolver for the A record of that domain. The query looks completely ordinary - a normal name, a normal record type. The resolver logs it and forwards it, because the name is unknown
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: The attacker’s name server answers
steps.caption: The attacker owns the domain and answers with a crafted IP address, 45.77.12.88 , and a TTL of 300 seconds. The answer looks like a boring hosting address. It is not: the attacker chose those numbers on purpose
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: The implant computes the port
steps.caption: The malware takes the first three octets of the answer - 45, 77 and 12 - and computes 45 × 77 + 12 = 3477 , the APT12-style formula from MITRE’s example. Nothing is on the wire yet; the port exists only inside the implant
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.caption: The implant fetches orders and reports results over the derived-port session. Small, regular transfers - exactly like any quiet management channel, and invisible to port-based blocking

steps.title: The port keeps changing
steps.caption: On the next check-in the attacker changes the answer to 91.204.16.5 , so the new port is 91 × 204 + 16 = 18580 . No static blocklist can keep up: the port is different after every answer

steps.title: The SOC correlates DNS and connections
steps.caption: The SOC joins Sysmon Event 22 (DNS query) with Event 3 (network connection) per process and finds the pattern: each connection’s port equals a function of the answer’s octets. The team blocks the domain and hunts every host that shows the same pair
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.
